figures.alt: A phone held almost touching a store's card reader, and a phone whose screen arrow points to a set of keys.

figures.caption: **Figure 1. The card runs on the reader's power.** The green arrow is the power going in. Only then can the chip answer.
figures.alt: The reader sends power to the card, and only then does the card's chip answer.

figures.caption: **Figure 2. How close is close.** Only a card inside the green tap zone wakes up. Roughly to scale.
figures.alt: A ruler from the reader. Only a card inside the first few centimeters wakes up. At a hand's width or a foot it stays asleep.

figures.caption: **Figure 3. The store gets a stand-in, not your card number.** Follow the green tags from your phone to your bank. Simplified.
figures.alt: Your phone sends a stand-in number to the store; only your bank can match it to your real card.

figures.caption: **Figure 4. A code that works once.** Each real tap sends a new code. A copy played back later is turned down, because the bank has already seen that code. Simplified.
figures.alt: Monday and Tuesday taps each send a different code and are approved. A copy of Monday's code is turned down.

figures.caption: **Figure 5. Swipe versus tap.** A swipe sends the same data every time, so a copy works again. A tap or chip sends a new code.
figures.alt: Swiping sends the same data each time, so a copy works again. Tapping or inserting sends a new code each time.

figures.caption: **Figure 6. Why a hidden reader gets nothing useful.** Read left to right: even a thief close enough to read your card gets a code the bank won't take again.
figures.alt: A thief must hold a reader almost touching your card, gets one code that works once, and the bank turns it down.

figures.caption: **Figure 7. Three cards, built three ways.** A bank card is built for a tap. A passport book has shielding in its cover. A passport card is made to be read from farther away, so it comes with its own sleeve.
figures.alt: A bank card needs no shield. A passport book is shielded when closed. A passport card should stay in its sleeve.

figures.caption: **Figure 8. The real risks, and what to do.** None of them is about the tap radio.
figures.alt: Three real risks, a skimmer at the pump, a lost phone and a scam caller, each with the fix.

figures.caption: **Figure 9. Your phone points the way.** It times a quick ping and reply with the tracker, then shows an arrow. Not to scale.
figures.alt: The phone pings the tracker on your keys, times the reply, and shows an arrow pointing to them.

figures.caption: **Figure 10. Two ways to judge distance.** Most Bluetooth gear guesses by how loud the signal sounds. Ultra Wideband times it, which is far more exact. Not to scale.
figures.alt: Bluetooth guesses from loudness, giving a wide circle. Ultra Wideband times a ping and reply, giving an exact spot.

figures.caption: **Figure 11. The car checks the timing.** A signal passed along from far away takes too long, so the car stays locked. Not to scale.
figures.alt: At the car, the phone's quick reply unlocks it. A signal relayed from indoors takes too long, so the car stays locked.
